abstract: >-
  An interaction is a difference between differences, and equal differences on one scale become unequal on another. Whether two effects interact therefore depends on the scale on which they are assumed to add, and in psychological research the observed response and the construct of interest often lie on different scales. Generalized linear models make this choice explicit through the link function, which is distinct from the outcome family that describes the response. Choosing a link is thus choosing what 'no interaction' means. A preregistered review of 2024 articles from five prominent psychology journals found interaction tests in 60% of 345 eligible articles. Among the 200 articles testing interactions on observed outcomes, 77% did not state the link function, and 72% applied Gaussian identity-link models to constrained outcomes. Worked examples and simulations of forced-choice accuracy with a chance floor, logit versus probit links, and sum scores show how a plausible-looking link can turn effects that are additive on one scale into a statistically significant interaction on another. A further simulation shows that residual checks, a link test, and AIC comparisons detect a wrong link only unevenly and do not by themselves decide which scale the scientific claim concerns. Interaction claims remain underspecified until researchers state, justify, and probe the scale on which no interaction is assumed.

##

Suppose we compare two groups of children, for instance a clinical and a neurotypical group, on a task. The groups differ in how many errors they make, and in both groups errors decrease with age. A researcher records error counts from children aged six to ten and analyzes them, as is common, with a Gaussian linear model that includes an age-by-group interaction. In @fig-simple-count-example (Panel A) the two fitted lines decline at different rates, and the gap between the groups is much wider at age six than at age ten. Is there an age-by-group interaction?

```{r}
#| label: fig-simple-count-example
#| fig-cap: "Simulated error counts for two groups of children aged 6 to 10, generated with the same age effect in both groups on the log of the expected error count. A Gaussian linear model fitted to the counts produces straight lines with different slopes, which suggests an age-by-group interaction. A Poisson model with a log link fitted to the same data produces curves that converge with age on the count scale and parallel lines on the log scale (where points show the log of non-zero counts), so the group gap shrinks on the count scale and stays constant on the log scale. Whether the pattern is an interaction depends on the scale on which effects are assumed to add."
#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.height: 3.2

set.seed(3)

N <- 250
d_count <- data.frame(
  age = round(runif(N, 6, 10), 1),
  condition = factor(rbinom(N, 1, .5), labels = c("Group A", "Group B"))
)

d_count$eta <- with(d_count, 2.6 - 0.55 * (age - 6) + 0.65 * (condition == "Group B"))
d_count$errors <- rpois(N, exp(d_count$eta))

fit_gauss <- lm(errors ~ age * condition, data = d_count)
fit_count <- glm(errors ~ age + condition, family = poisson(link = "log"), data = d_count)

count_pred <- expand.grid(age = seq(6, 10, length.out = 200), condition = levels(d_count$condition))
g <- predict(fit_gauss, newdata = count_pred, se.fit = TRUE)
p <- predict(fit_count, newdata = count_pred, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)

scale_levels <- c("A. Gaussian identity: errors", "B. Poisson log: log(errors)", "C. Poisson log: errors")

pred_two <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    count_pred, scale = scale_levels[1],
    fit = g$fit,
    lower = g$fit - 1.96 * g$se.fit,
    upper = g$fit + 1.96 * g$se.fit
  ),
  data.frame(
    count_pred, scale = scale_levels[2],
    fit = p$fit,
    lower = p$fit - 1.96 * p$se.fit,
    upper = p$fit + 1.96 * p$se.fit
  ),
  data.frame(
    count_pred, scale = scale_levels[3],
    fit = exp(p$fit),
    lower = exp(p$fit - 1.96 * p$se.fit),
    upper = exp(p$fit + 1.96 * p$se.fit)
  )
)
pred_two$scale <- factor(pred_two$scale, levels = scale_levels)

d_pos <- d_count[d_count$errors > 0, ]
points_two <- rbind(
  data.frame(age = d_count$age, condition = d_count$condition, y = d_count$errors, scale = scale_levels[1]),
  data.frame(age = d_pos$age, condition = d_pos$condition, y = log(d_pos$errors), scale = scale_levels[2]),
  data.frame(age = d_count$age, condition = d_count$condition, y = d_count$errors, scale = scale_levels[3])
)
points_two$scale <- factor(points_two$scale, levels = scale_levels)

ggplot(points_two, aes(age, y, color = condition, shape = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = .5) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = pred_two,
    aes(x = age, ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = condition, group = condition),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = .18, color = NA
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = pred_two,
    aes(x = age, y = fit, linetype = condition, group = condition),
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Group A" = "#0072B2", "Group B" = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Group A" = "#0072B2", "Group B" = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = NULL, color = NULL, fill = NULL, shape = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  (ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = (11), base_family = "") +
    ggplot2::theme(
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(
        face = "bold",
        size = (11) + 1,
        margin = ggplot2::margin(b = 3)
      ),
      plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text(
        size = (11) - 1,
        color = "grey25",
        margin = ggplot2::margin(b = 6)
      ),
      axis.title = ggplot2::element_text(size = (11)),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = (11) - 1, color = "grey20"),
      strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", size = (11) - 1),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = ggplot2::element_text(size = (11) - 1),
      legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = (11) - 1),
      legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.25, "lines"),
      panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_line(linewidth = 0.25, color = "grey88"),
      panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.9, "lines"),
      plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(6, 8, 6, 8)
    )) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

An interaction is a difference between differences, so the question is whether the group difference itself changes with age. Since the gap narrows as the children grow older, the natural conclusion is that age and group interact. The data in @fig-simple-count-example, however, were generated without any interaction. Errors follow a Poisson process in which age and group add on the log scale, so the two groups share the same age slope on that scale. A Poisson model with a log link recovers this structure, and on the log scale its fitted lines are parallel (@fig-simple-count-example, Panel B). Mapped back onto the count scale, the same model produces two curves that converge with age, because a constant difference on the log scale is a constant ratio on the count scale, and the absolute gap between the groups therefore narrows as errors decline (@fig-simple-count-example, Panel C). Whether an interaction is present thus depends on the scale on which effects are assumed to add. Additivity on the log scale implies non-parallel curves on the count scale, and additivity on the count scale would imply non-parallel curves on the log scale.

This ambiguity extends far beyond this single illustration, as interaction hypotheses are widespread in psychological research and often represent the central target of inquiry [@rohrer2021; @domingue2024; @mccabe2022]. Whenever researchers ask whether an effect is moderated, or whether it holds only under certain conditions, they are asserting that the impact of one variable depends on another.

In psychology, this scale dependence has a characteristic source in measurement. Researchers often conceptualize constructs such as cognitive ability or symptom severity as continuous latent dimensions [@embretsonReise2000; @wagenmakers2012]. Those dimensions are rarely observed directly; what reaches the data are bounded, discrete quantities, such as counts, ratings, and accuracy scores that carry floors, ceilings, and chance levels. Each measurement scale imposes its own mapping from the latent dimension to the observed response. Where the mapping compresses, a constant effect on the latent dimension appears as a shrinking effect on the observed response. A group or condition closer to a bound has less room to move, and can look less affected by a manipulation than one farther from the bounds (e.g., @fig-simple-count-example).

Generalized linear models (GLMs) make this mapping explicit and give it a standard vocabulary [@nelderwedderburn1972; @mccullaghnelder1989], separating two choices that are easy to conflate, (1) the outcome family, which describes the response, and (2) the link function, which sets the scale on which effects combine (Box 1).

::: {.callout-note title="Box 1: Generalized linear models: outcome family and link function" icon="false"}
The *outcome family* is the distribution assumed for the response. It defines which values the outcome can take and how observations vary around their expectation. The *link function*, $g(\cdot)$, maps the expected outcome, $\mu_i = E(Y_i)$, onto the linear predictor, $\eta_i$, the scale on which the model is additive. With two predictors and their interaction term, $$g(\mu_i) = \eta_i, \qquad \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \beta_2 Z_i + \beta_3 X_i Z_i.$$

The inverse link, $g^{-1}(\cdot)$, maps this additive structure back onto the expected response. Its familiar role is to keep expected values within the admissible range of a constrained outcome: $\exp(\eta)$ keeps expected counts positive, and the inverse logit keeps probabilities between 0 and 1. Less obviously, this also fixes what the absence of an interaction, $\beta_3 = 0$, means in the fitted model. The product-term coefficient $\beta_3$ is therefore an interaction on the link scale. A response-scale interaction is a different quantity: a difference between expected differences on the observed outcome, for example, whether the group difference in expected errors changes with age in @fig-simple-count-example. Unless the link is the identity, the two quantities can disagree [@ainorton2003; @mccabe2022; @mize2019]. Each family has a canonical link, which is the one that arises directly from the family's mathematical form, but it is a convenient default and other links are legitimate. A Gaussian linear model is the special case that combines a Gaussian family with an identity link, so the additive scale and the response scale coincide and the scale question is invisible. The model behind @fig-simple-count-example is a Poisson family with a log link. The family respects that errors are non-negative counts, and the link places additivity on the log scale.
:::

Often the outcome family is chosen with care while the link function is left at its software default, fixing the scale of additivity without deliberation. Two models can share a family and still place additivity on different scales. For example, a Gamma family suits response times; within that family, a log link makes effects additive on the log of the mean response time, a proportional change, and the canonical inverse link makes them additive in reciprocal means, a change in speed. A binomial family fits correct-versus-incorrect responses and leaves the link open among logit, probit, chance-corrected, and other forms.

The scale dependence of interactions has long been recognized. @loftus1978 showed that interactions involving response probabilities are meaningful only relative to a mapping between observed and theoretical scales; @cox1984 formalized interaction as a model-relative concept tied to transformation and interpretation. @busemeyer1983 carried the same point into the measurement model, where the conclusion about how two variables combine depends on the model assumed to link responses to the quantities they measure. @lubinski1990 showed that the specification choices alone can produce the appearance of an interaction where the generating process contains none.

@wagenmakers2012 revisited the distinction between "removable" and "nonremovable" interactions. A removable interaction can disappear under some monotonic transformation of the dependent variable, whereas a nonremovable one cannot. In this regard, @dunnanderson2026 developed a removability test for linear models, while @rohrer2021 showed that the same interaction can be positive, null, or negative depending on the scale chosen for the outcome, so the appropriate test follows from the scale on which the hypothesis is posed. Rimpler and colleagues [-@rimpler2026] added that a product term assumes one predictor's effect changes at a constant rate across levels of the other, and so misrepresents any dependence that does not take that form, such as a threshold effect. Because the product-term coefficient of a GLM refers to the link scale (Box 1), a question about the response scale is answered with marginal effects [@ainorton2003; @mccabe2022; @mize2019; @rohrer2026]. 

Domingue and colleagues [-@domingue2024] demonstrated that outcome-model misspecification can produce false interaction findings for binary, count, and censored outcomes, and @liddellkruschke2018 showed that treating ordinal responses as metric can inflate error rates for interactions. Czado and Santner, and later Yu and Huang, studied the inferential consequences of link misspecification in binary GLMs and GLMMs [@czadosantner1992; @yuhuang2019]. 

Although this literature spans decades, to our knowledge no study has attempted to quantify how often applied psychological research makes explicit the outcome family and link that define the no-interaction baseline. The present article approaches that gap from two directions. We first document current practice with a preregistered review of recent empirical articles in five prominent psychology journals, quantifying how often interactions are tested, how often the outcome family and link function are made explicit, and which response formats predominate. Using the GLM framework, we then distinguish outcome family, link function, and target metric, and examine three cases: forced-choice accuracy with a chance floor, the choice between logit and probit links, and sum scores. Simulations quantify how often an inadequate link turns a purely additive structure into a statistically significant interaction, and whether standard diagnostics detect the misspecification.

# Current Practice in Psychological Interaction Testing: A Preregistered Review

```{r review-section-load-data}
#| include: false

find_repo_file <- function(...) {
  rel <- file.path(...)
  candidates <- c(rel, file.path("..", rel))
  hit <- candidates[file.exists(candidates)]
  if (length(hit) == 0) {
    stop(
      "Cannot find required file: ", rel, ".\n",
      "Looked in: ", paste(candidates, collapse = "; "), ".\n",
      "Run the corresponding script before rendering paper.qmd."
    )
  }
  hit[1]
}

review_table_path <- find_repo_file("tables", "review-summary.csv")
outcome_table_path <- find_repo_file("tables", "review-outcome-types.csv")
agreement_table_path <- find_repo_file("tables", "review-intercoder-agreement.csv")
journal_table_path <- find_repo_file("tables", "review-by-journal.csv")
screening_flow_path <- find_repo_file("tables", "review-screening-flow.csv")

review_table <- read.csv(review_table_path)
outcome_table <- read.csv(outcome_table_path)
agreement_table <- read.csv(agreement_table_path)
journal_table <- read.csv(journal_table_path)
screening_flow_table <- read.csv(screening_flow_path)

# eligibility row of Table 1: denominator is the number screened for eligibility (not the number eligible)
n_screened <- screening_flow_table$n[screening_flow_table$step == "articles screened for eligibility"]
i_elig <- which(review_table$row_id == "eligible_empirical")
review_table$quantity[i_elig] <- "Articles meeting eligibility criteria"
review_table$denominator_n[i_elig] <- n_screened
review_table$percent[i_elig] <- round(100 * review_table$n[i_elig] / n_screened, 1)
review_table[i_elig, c("ci_low", "ci_high")] <- round(100 * prop.test(review_table$n[i_elig], n_screened, correct = FALSE)$conf.int, 1) # Wilson

get_review_row <- function(row_id, data = review_table) {
  if (!"row_id" %in% names(data)) {
    stop("Review summary table must contain a row_id column. Re-run scripts/01-review-descriptives.R before rendering.")
  }
  idx <- which(data$row_id == row_id)
  if (length(idx) != 1) {
    stop("Could not uniquely identify review row_id: ", row_id)
  }
  data[idx, ]
}

n_eligible <- get_review_row("eligible_empirical")
n_interactions <- get_review_row("testing_interactions")
n_observed <- get_review_row("observed_outcome_interactions")
n_latent_only <- get_review_row("latent_only_interactions")
n_non_identity <- get_review_row("non_identity_link")
n_explicit <- get_review_row("explicit_link")
n_non_identity_not_explicit <- get_review_row("non_identity_not_explicit")
n_identity_only_not_explicit <- get_review_row("identity_only_not_explicit")
n_incorrect_identity <- get_review_row("incorrect_identity")
n_significant_incorrect_identity <- get_review_row("significant_incorrect_identity")

get_outcome_row <- function(pattern, data = outcome_table) {
  idx <- grep(pattern, data$outcome_type, ignore.case = TRUE)
  if (length(idx) != 1) {
    stop("Could not uniquely identify outcome row: ", pattern)
  }
  data[idx, ]
}

get_agreement_row <- function(variable, data = agreement_table) {
  idx <- which(data$variable == variable)
  if (length(idx) != 1) {
    stop("Could not uniquely identify agreement variable: ", variable)
  }
  data[idx, ]
}

get_journal_row <- function(journal, data = journal_table) {
  idx <- which(data$journal == journal)
  if (length(idx) != 1) {
    stop("Could not uniquely identify journal row: ", journal)
  }
  data[idx, ]
}

outcome_binary <- get_outcome_row("Binary")
outcome_sum <- get_outcome_row("Sum scores")
outcome_ordinal <- get_outcome_row("Ordinal")
outcome_rt <- get_outcome_row("Response times")
outcome_neural <- get_outcome_row("Neural")
outcome_difference <- get_outcome_row("Difference")
outcome_correlations <- get_outcome_row("Correlations")
outcome_counts <- get_outcome_row("Counts")

agree_non_identity <- get_agreement_row("Uses_non_identity_link_function")
agree_explicit <- get_agreement_row("Explicit_link_function")
agree_incorrect_identity <- get_agreement_row("Incorrect_identity_link_function")
agree_significant <- get_agreement_row("Finds_significant_interaction")

journal_psychmed <- get_journal_row("Psychological Medicine")
journal_min_incorrect_identity <- journal_table[which.min(journal_table$incorrect_identity_percent_interaction), ]
journal_max_incorrect_identity <- journal_table[which.max(journal_table$incorrect_identity_percent_interaction), ]
journal_min_interaction <- journal_table[which.min(journal_table$interaction_testing_percent_of_eligible), ]
journal_max_interaction <- journal_table[which.max(journal_table$interaction_testing_percent_of_eligible), ]

fmt_ci <- function(row) {
  paste0(row$percent, "%, 95% CI [", row$ci_low, ", ", row$ci_high, "]")
}

fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  out <- ifelse(is.na(x), "--", formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "f", digits = digits))
  out
}

fmt_count <- function(x) {
  ifelse(is.na(x), "--", formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "f", digits = 0))
}

fmt_agreement_kappa <- function(row) {
  paste0(
    fmt_num(100 * row$agreement, 1), "% agreement, kappa = ",
    fmt_num(row$kappa, 2)
  )
}

fmt_yes_margins <- function(row) {
  if (all(c("coder1_yes_percent", "coder2_yes_percent") %in% names(row))) {
    return(paste0(
      fmt_num(row$coder1_yes_percent, 1), "% / ",
      fmt_num(row$coder2_yes_percent, 1), "%"
    ))
  }
  n <- row$n_double_coded
  coder1_yes <- 100 * (row$n_10 + row$n_11) / n
  coder2_yes <- 100 * (row$n_01 + row$n_11) / n
  paste0(fmt_num(coder1_yes, 1), "% / ", fmt_num(coder2_yes, 1), "%")
}

fmt_ci_cols <- function(low, high, digits = 3) {
  ifelse(
    is.na(low) | is.na(high),
    "--",
    paste0("[", fmt_num(low, digits), ", ", fmt_num(high, digits), "]")
  )
}

review_display_table <- function(dat) {
  out <- data.frame(
    Quantity = dat$quantity,
    n = fmt_count(dat$n),
    `Denom.` = fmt_count(dat$denominator_n),
    `%` = paste0(fmt_num(dat$percent, 1), "%"),
    `95% CI (%)` = paste0("[", fmt_num(dat$ci_low, 1), ", ", fmt_num(dat$ci_high, 1), "]"),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
  out
}

simulation_display_table <- function(dat, effect_col = NULL, include_scale = FALSE) {
  out <- data.frame(.row = seq_len(nrow(dat)), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if ("Scenario" %in% names(dat)) out$Scenario <- dat$Scenario
  if ("Generating link" %in% names(dat)) out$`Generating link` <- dat$`Generating link`
  if ("Model" %in% names(dat)) out$Model <- dat$Model
  if ("Fitted link" %in% names(dat)) out$`Fitted link` <- dat$`Fitted link`
  if ("Link status" %in% names(dat)) out$`Link status` <- dat$`Link status`
  if ("Rate type" %in% names(dat)) out$`Rate type` <- dat$`Rate type`
  if (include_scale && "Units for group-gap change" %in% names(dat)) {
    out$Scale <- ifelse(grepl("latent", dat$`Units for group-gap change`), "latent theta", "sum score")
  }
  if ("Successful fits" %in% names(dat)) out$Fits <- fmt_count(dat$`Successful fits`)
  if ("Rejections" %in% names(dat)) out$Reject <- fmt_count(dat$Rejections)
  if ("Rejection rate" %in% names(dat)) {
    out$`Rejection rate` <- fmt_num(dat$`Rejection rate`, 3)
  }
  if (all(c("CI low", "CI high") %in% names(dat))) {
    out$`95% CI` <- fmt_ci_cols(dat$`CI low`, dat$`CI high`, 3)
  }
  if (!is.null(effect_col) && effect_col %in% names(dat)) {
    out$`Median gap change` <- fmt_num(dat[[effect_col]], 3)
  }
  if ("Median interaction coefficient" %in% names(dat)) {
    out$`Median beta interaction` <- fmt_num(dat$`Median interaction coefficient`, 3)
  }
  if ("Median interaction SE" %in% names(dat)) {
    out$`Median SE` <- fmt_num(dat$`Median interaction SE`, 3)
  }
  out$.row <- NULL
  out
}

rate_display_table <- function(dat) {
  data.frame(
    Quantity = dat$Quantity,
    Fits = fmt_count(dat$`Successful fits`),
    Sig = fmt_count(dat$`Significant tests`),
    Rate = fmt_num(dat$Rate, 3),
    `95% CI` = fmt_ci_cols(dat$`CI low`, dat$`CI high`, 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

```

The review asks how often psychological articles test interactions, and how often they make the outcome family and link function explicit enough for a reader to know which interaction claim was tested. The coding is descriptive. It documents reporting practice and makes no judgment on the correctness of any substantive conclusion.

## Review Method

The protocol was preregistered before any record was screened (<https://osf.io/bdu73/>), together with the coding data dictionary. The essentials are given here; the full protocol, sampling frame, and reliability are in Supplement A.

Following the preregistration, we sampled one journal from each of five areas: *Psychological Science* (general), *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General* (experimental), *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* (social), *Developmental Science* (developmental), and *Psychological Medicine* (clinical). The five were selected on preregistered discretionary criteria: a first-quartile 2023 Impact Factor, a broad rather than narrowly specialized scope, not primarily publishing reviews, and strong reputation in their field, as jointly judged by the coauthors. From each journal's full set of 2024 articles in Scopus, records were screened in a fixed random order until 40 eligible articles testing at least one interaction on an observed outcome were reached, yielding `r n_observed$n` coded articles. The preregistered stopping rule referred to interaction-testing articles in general; the restriction to observed outcomes was introduced during implementation. Because screening stopped at a fixed number of coded articles, the number of records screened, and therefore the denominator of the eligibility proportion, varied across journals. Eligible articles were empirical reports of original research; reviews, meta-analyses, editorials, theoretical and qualitative-only articles, replication-only studies, and psychometric validation studies were excluded. The use of latent-variable or structural-equation models was not a reason for exclusion. Articles whose interaction tests all concerned latent outcomes did not count toward the 40 per journal, because our family and link coding was defined for observed outcomes. Note that latent-variable models do not remove the scale problem per se, but move part of it to the measurement model and the definition of the latent scale.  We treat this restriction as a deviation from the protocol and retain the resulting sample rather than reconstructing the point at which screening would otherwise have stopped. It concerned `r n_latent_only$n` of the `r n_interactions$n` eligible interaction-testing articles; articles combining latent-variable analyses with at least one observed-outcome interaction were coded.

Each of the coded articles was independently coded by two researchers, with disagreements resolved by discussion or by consulting the other coauthors. Generative AI tools were used only as an optional aid to locate passages within an article; all coding used in the review is human.

For each article, the coders recorded five things: whether at least one tested interaction used a non-identity link; whether the link function of at least one model was explicit; whether at least one interaction applied a Gaussian-identity analysis to a constrained outcome; whether at least one such interaction was statistically significant, or interpreted analogously in a Bayesian analysis; and which response-variable types were analyzed. 

By a Gaussian-identity analysis on a constrained outcome we mean a model with a Gaussian family and an identity link (e.g., ANOVA, linear regression, linear mixed model) applied to an outcome with formal constraints, such as bounds, discreteness, positivity, or a known chance level. We applied this flag only when those constraints were clear from the description of the outcome, and not when the observed score was explicitly justified as the target metric, in which case identity-link additivity can be a defensible choice, as discussed in the section on sensitivity analysis.

Interrater agreement on the double-coded records was high (Cohen's $\kappa$ between `r fmt_num(min(agreement_table$kappa), 2)` and `r fmt_num(max(agreement_table$kappa), 2)`). Supplement A, Section S2, reports the preregistered variable definitions, the operational coding rules including borderline cases, per-variable agreement and coder margins, and the by-journal results.

## Review Findings

First, interaction testing was common. Of the `r n_eligible$denominator_n` articles screened, `r n_eligible$n` met the eligibility criteria, of which `r n_interactions$n` tested at least one interaction (`r fmt_num(n_interactions$percent, 1)`%). Because the number of records screened depended on the stopping rule, the per-journal proportions are the more informative summary. They ranged from `r fmt_num(journal_min_interaction$interaction_testing_percent_of_eligible, 1)`% in  `r journal_min_interaction$journal`  to  `r fmt_num(journal_max_interaction$interaction_testing_percent_of_eligible, 1)`% in  `r journal_max_interaction$journal`. Of the interaction-testing articles, `r n_latent_only$n` (`r fmt_num(n_latent_only$percent, 1)`%) tested interactions only on latent outcomes, and the remaining `r n_observed$n` formed the coded sample described below.

Second, the link function was rarely stated. Of the `r n_observed$n` coded articles, `r n_non_identity$n` (`r str_extract(fmt_ci(n_non_identity), "\\d+%")`) tested at least one interaction with a model that implies a non-identity link, such as a logistic regression or a binomial generalized linear mixed model. In `r n_non_identity_not_explicit$n` of these `r n_non_identity$n` articles (`r fmt_num(n_non_identity_not_explicit$percent, 0)`%), the report named only the family or the type of model and did not state the link. In these cases, the reader had to infer the link, typically from the software default. Overall, `r n_explicit$n` articles (`r str_extract(fmt_ci(n_explicit), "\\d+%")`) stated the link of at least one model, which was not necessarily the model used to test the interaction. We counted the link as stated when the report named it, either directly or through a model name that identifies it, such as "logistic regression" for the logit and "probit regression" for the probit. We also accepted "Poisson regression", although it names a family, because the term conventionally refers to a model for counts with a log link, and other links are rarely used with the Poisson family. 

This rule is looser than the preregistered one, which required the link to be declared and treated naming a family or a generalized linear model as insufficient, and under the preregistered rule the count would be lower. Most of the articles without an explicit link (`r n_identity_only_not_explicit$n` of `r n_identity_only_not_explicit$denominator_n`) tested interactions only with ANOVA, ordinary regression, or linear mixed models. The names of these models also identify the link, which is the identity, but we did not count them as explicit. Because these models are the default analysis in psychology, we did not take their use as evidence that the authors had considered the scale on which the interaction was tested. The same argument could be made for logistic regression, which is the default analysis for binary outcomes, and authors who name it may also have chosen it by convention, without attention to the scale of the interaction. The count of explicit links therefore reflects reporting practice, as do the other coded variables, and cannot establish whether the authors considered the scale of the interaction.

Third, constrained outcomes were often analyzed on the identity scale. Among the `r n_observed$n` coded articles, `r n_incorrect_identity$n` included at least one Gaussian-identity analysis on a constrained observed outcome (`r str_extract(fmt_ci(n_incorrect_identity),"\\d+%")`). Of these `r n_incorrect_identity$n` cases, `r n_significant_incorrect_identity$n` reported at least one statistically significant interaction (`r fmt_num(n_significant_incorrect_identity$percent, 0)`%). Because significance was coded only within the flagged analyses, this proportion describes those articles alone, and across all coded articles `r fmt_num(100 * n_significant_incorrect_identity$n / n_observed$n, 0)`% combined a constrained outcome, an identity-link analysis, and a significant interaction claim. @tbl-current-practice summarizes these results.

The interval on the eligibility row is given for completeness only, because screening stopped at 40 coded articles per journal and the number of records screened was not fixed by design."

The pattern was present across the sampled journals, where the proportion of coded articles with a Gaussian-identity analysis on a constrained observed outcome ranged from `r fmt_num(journal_min_incorrect_identity$incorrect_identity_percent_interaction, 0)`% in `r journal_min_incorrect_identity$journal` to `r fmt_num(journal_max_incorrect_identity$incorrect_identity_percent_interaction, 0)`% in `r journal_max_incorrect_identity$journal` (Supplement A). 

The outcomes used in interaction analyses were heterogeneous. The most common broad, non-exclusive categories (@tbl-review-outcome-types) were binary, accuracy, or proportion outcomes (`r outcome_binary$n` articles), sum scores or composites (`r outcome_sum$n` articles), ordinal, Likert, or rating outcomes (`r outcome_ordinal$n` articles), response times or durations (`r outcome_rt$n` articles), neural or physiological measures (`r outcome_neural$n` articles), difference or distance scores (`r outcome_difference$n` articles), counts or error counts (`r outcome_counts$n` articles), and correlations or associations (`r outcome_correlations$n` articles). These broad categories combine the more detailed labels used to classify the response variables during coding. The operational definitions and decision rules used to distinguish them are reported in Supplement A.

## What the Present Review Shows, What It Does Not

In these journals, then, interaction tests are common, the scale on which no interaction is assumed is rarely stated, and identity-link analyses of constrained outcomes are frequent. Bounded outcomes dominated, with binary, accuracy, or proportion outcomes, sum scores, and ordinal ratings together appearing in 152 of the `r n_observed$n` coded articles (76%). For such outcomes additivity on the observed scale is a strong assumption, and treating them as metric can distort estimates, error rates, and interaction conclusions [@liddellkruschke2018; @burknervuorre2019].

We cannot determine from this review how often published interactions are scale artifacts, because that judgment requires knowing the scale on which the data-generating process is additive. The removability test of @dunnanderson2026 requires cell-level summaries and error estimates, which the reviewed articles often did not report, and it has no straightforward extension to the mixed-effects models that many of them used. The remainder of the paper therefore turns to simulations, where the generating process is known by construction, and focuses on the binomial and aggregated responses that dominated the corpus, including sums of binary or ordinal items.

# The Link Function Problem in Three Common Cases

Here we examine how often a process that is additive on its generating scale yields a significant interaction when modeled on another scale, even when the family and response bounds are correctly specified. We consider three cases:

1.  *Forced-Choice Accuracy*: This case holds the binomial outcome family fixed and evaluates whether the link function must explicitly encode a task-implied chance floor (e.g., a .50 guessing threshold).
2.  *Within-Family Link Choice (Logit vs. Probit)*: This case holds both the binary family and the 0-to-1 bounds fixed, showing that even choosing between these two standard link functions with the same bounds alters the results.
3.  *Sum Scores*: This case holds the latent generating process fixed and evaluates whether the bounded total shows an interaction that the latent scale does not.

The three simulations share the same estimand, methods, and performance measure. Data are generated with no product term on the generating scale, so the estimand, the product term on that scale, is zero by construction. Models assuming additivity on the generating scale and on plausible alternative scales are fitted to the same data, and the performance measure is the proportion of replications in which the product term is significant at $\alpha = .05$. For the matched model this is the *nominal rejection rate*. A product term estimated under a mismatched model is a genuine property of that model's scale [@loftus1978; @cox1984; @domingue2024; @mccabe2022], correct where it is computed and misleading only when the claim is carried to the generating scale. Because that scale is known in a simulation, we call such a result a *pseudo-interaction*, and its rejection rate the *pseudo-interaction detection rate*. 

The scenarios were chosen to represent plausible psychological data. Each reproduces a common interaction-testing situation, in which two well-established and large main effects, for example a group difference combined with a condition effect or a developmental trend, raise the question of whether one effect moderates the other. Most scenarios set these effects strong enough to push expected values close to a floor, ceiling, or chance level while keeping them inside the observed range, which is where link curvature acts most strongly, and scenarios away from the bounds serve as a comparison. Technical details are reported in Supplement A, and Supplement B reports a broader sensitivity atlas that varies sample size, main-effect magnitude, the intercept, and selected design parameters. A final simulation, in the next section, examines whether standard diagnostics identify the misspecified link.

Every scenario of every simulation was replicated 3,000 times, with a new dataset in each replication. A rate near .05 therefore has a Monte Carlo standard error of about 0.4 percentage points, and Supplement A reports Wilson 95% confidence intervals for every rate. All analyses were conducted in R [@rcoreteam2025, version 4.5.1]. Mixed models were fitted with `lme4` [@bates2015] and `glmmTMB` [@brooks2017], the chance-corrected link was taken from `psyphy` [@knoblauch2023psyphy], and residual diagnostics used `DHARMa` [@hartig2024]. Package versions are pinned with `renv` [@ushey2025renv].

read_required_table <- function(file, script_hint) {
  path <- find_repo_file("tables", file)
  dat <- read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if (nrow(dat) == 0) {
    stop("The table ", path, " exists but has zero rows. Re-run ", script_hint, ".")
  }
  dat
}

select_required_columns <- function(dat, cols) {
  missing <- setdiff(cols, names(dat))
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop(
      "The following required columns were not found: ",
      paste(missing, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }
  dat[, cols, drop = FALSE]
}

rename_columns <- function(dat, labels) {
  names(dat)[match(names(labels), names(dat))] <- unname(labels)
  dat
}

# Inline row lookups must hit exactly one row. A label that no longer matches the
# summary tables would otherwise return a zero-length value that knitr renders as
# an empty string, silently dropping the number from the text.
require_single <- function(value, what) {
  if (length(value) != 1) {
    stop(
      "Inline lookup ", what, " matched ", length(value),
      " values instead of 1. Check that the label matches the summary table."
    )
  }
  value
}

    "quantitative_description",
    "variability_summary"
  )
)

cap_first <- function(x) paste0(toupper(substr(x, 1, 1)), substring(x, 2))

diagnostic_scenario_display_table <- function(dat) {
  # same checks on the correctly specified model fitted to the same data
  cal <- diagnostic_calibration_correct
  dh <- grepl("^DHARMa", cal$diagnostic)
  dh_min <- tapply(cal$flagging_rate[dh], cal$scenario[dh], min)[dat$Case]
  dh_max <- tapply(cal$flagging_rate[dh], cal$scenario[dh], max)[dat$Case]
  pg <- tapply(cal$flagging_rate[!dh], cal$scenario[!dh], max)[dat$Case]
  data.frame(
    Scenario = dat$Case,
    `Link: correct (generating) $\\rightarrow$ wrong (fitted)` = paste(dat$`Target link`, "$\\rightarrow$", dat$`Fitted link`),
    `Pseudo-interaction rate, wrong link` = fmt_num(dat$`Pseudo-interaction detection`, 2),
    `DHARMa flagging rate, correct / wrong link` = paste0(
      fmt_num(dh_min, 2), "--", fmt_num(dh_max, 2), " / ",
      fmt_num(dat$`DHARMa min`, 2), "--", fmt_num(dat$`DHARMa max`, 2)
    ),
    `Pregibon flagging rate, correct / wrong link` = ifelse(
      dat$Case == pregibon_na_scenario,
      "N.I.",
      paste0(fmt_num(pg, 2), " / ", fmt_num(dat$`Pregibon check`, 2))
    ),
    `AIC prefers correct link` = fmt_num(dat$`AIC favors target`, 2),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

dg_lookup <- function(case, col) {
  if (!col %in% names(diagnostic_scenarios)) {
    stop(
      "Unknown diagnostic scenario column: ", col,
      ". Available columns: ",
      paste(names(diagnostic_scenarios), collapse = ", ")
    )
  }
  require_single(
    diagnostic_scenarios[diagnostic_scenarios$Case == case, col, drop = TRUE],
    paste0("diagnostic_scenarios[", case, " / ", col, "]")
  )
}

dg_n <- function(case) dg_lookup(case, "Replications")

}
dg_range <- function(col) {
  v <- 100 * diagnostic_scenarios[[col]]
  sprintf("%d%% to %d%%", round(min(v, na.rm = TRUE)), round(max(v, na.rm = TRUE)))
}

# Replications attempted per diagnostic scenario, before any convergence loss.
n_rep_diagnostic <- max(table(diagnostic_replications$scenario))

# Participants in the binary diagnostic scenarios (see scripts/04-diagnostic-worked-example.R).
dg_N_binary <- 300
dg_val <- function(case, col, digits = 1) fmt_num(dg_lookup(case, col), digits)

# Correct-link flagging in the chance-floor scenario versus all other scenarios.
cal <- diagnostic_calibration_correct
cal_cf <- cal$scenario == "Chance-floor accuracy"
cal_dharma <- grepl("^DHARMa", cal$diagnostic)
cal_cf_dharma_max <- round(100 * max(cal$flagging_rate[cal_cf & cal_dharma]))
cal_cf_pregibon <- round(100 * max(cal$flagging_rate[cal_cf & !cal_dharma]))
cal_other_max <- fmt_num(100 * max(cal$flagging_rate[!cal_cf]), 1)

## Forced-Choice Accuracy and the Non-Zero Chance Floor

If a participant answers $Y_i$ of $k$ trials correctly, a binomial sampling model, $Y_i \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(k, p_i)$, is the natural starting point. The family requires the expected accuracy to lie between 0 and 1. When guessing is a plausible process for the task, the range that matters is narrower, since a participant who knows nothing still gets a share $c$ of the trials right, $c = .50$ in a two-alternative or true/false task and $c = 1/m$ with $m$ alternatives, so expected accuracy lies between $c$ and 1, even though observed proportions can fall below $c$ through sampling variation. Accuracy data of this kind are analyzed in several ways in practice, on the raw proportion scale with a Gaussian identity model, with a standard binomial logit or probit, and, less often, with a link that encodes the chance floor.

These specifications differ in which of the two ranges they impose. The Gaussian identity model imposes neither, since it ignores the trial process, assumes additivity in percentage-correct units, and can predict outside the 0-to-1 range. The other two keep the binomial family and differ only in the link. The standard logit or probit, $p_i = F(\eta_i)$ with $F$ the logistic or standard-normal CDF, holds expected accuracy between 0 and 1 and places the lower asymptote at 0, whereas the chance-corrected link maps the linear predictor onto the narrower interval from $c$ to 1,
$p_i = c + (1 - c)F(\eta_i)$, which for $c = .50$ becomes $p_i = .50 + .50\,F(\eta_i)$. An interaction term in the standard model therefore tests additivity over the full 0-to-1 range, whereas the same term in the chance-corrected model tests additivity on a performance-above-chance scale, so the same four cell probabilities can imply different interactions on the three scales (@fig-motivating-example).

![A minimal $2 \times 2$ design crosses a condition (x-axis) with a group (color), shown on three scales. The four cell probabilities are identical in every panel; only the scale on which the interaction is evaluated changes. The data were generated with no condition-by-group interaction on the chance-corrected logit scale, which has a $.50$ chance floor, so the interaction coefficient is exactly zero on that scale. The same cells imply a positive interaction on the standard logit scale and a negative interaction on the raw probability scale. Light horizontal lines are equally spaced on each panel's own link scale, so equal steps on that scale map to unequal steps on the probability axis.](../figs/motivating-example.pdf){#fig-motivating-example}

The chance-corrected link is most defensible when the chance level is known from the task design, guessing is a plausible lower-bound process, and below-chance performance is not substantively meaningful for the target claim. In the simplest case, the chance level can be fixed by design, for example $c = .50$ in a two-alternative task. In other cases, analysts may estimate the lower asymptote or report sensitivity analyses over plausible values of $c$. Lapses, response biases, item heterogeneity, changes across trials, or systematic below-chance performance may instead require richer psychometric solutions such as item-response models [e.g., @embretsonReise2000; @wichmann2001; @knoblauch2012]. For example, the 3-parameter logistic Item Response Theory model estimates a guessing parameter for each item, where the chance-corrected link fixes a single chance level for the whole design [@embretsonReise2000]. The chance-corrected link is thus a design-level approximation, and item-level measurement models remain the appropriate tool when the data and the scientific question call for that additional structure.

### Simulation 1: Design and Results

```{r}
#| label: forced-choice-inline
#| include: false

# Design constants for Simulation 1 (see scripts/03a-simulation-forced-choice.R).
sim_N <- 250
sim_k <- 20
n_rep <- max(forced_choice_sim$`Fits attempted`)

# >>> NEW CODE (inline values for Simulation 1 results) >>>
fc_lookup <- function(scn, mdl, col) {
  require_single(
    forced_choice_sim[
      forced_choice_sim$Scenario == scn & forced_choice_sim$Model == mdl,
      col, drop = TRUE
    ],
    paste0("forced_choice_sim[", scn, " / ", mdl, " / ", col, "]")
  )
}
fc_rate <- function(scn, mdl) round(100 * fc_lookup(scn, mdl, "Primary rejection rate"))
fc_pct_range <- function(v) sprintf("%d%% to %d%%", round(100 * min(v)), round(100 * max(v)))

# Matched chance-corrected model: nominal rate, fit problems, and the rate an
# analyst would obtain by pooling acceptable and flagged fits.
fc_cc <- forced_choice_sim[forced_choice_sim$Model == "Chance-corrected binomial logit", ]
fc_alt <- forced_choice_sim[forced_choice_sim$Model != "Chance-corrected binomial logit", ]
fc_cc_pooled <- with(fc_cc,
  (`Rejections, acceptable fits` + `Apparent rejections, flagged fits`) /
    (`Finite p-values, acceptable fits` + `Finite p-values, flagged fits`)
)
```

Simulation 1 asks whether models that ignore the chance floor detect a product term that is zero on the chance-corrected scale. Three scenarios differ only in overall performance, set by shifting the fixed intercept so that expected accuracy lies closer to the .50 floor (lower performance), in the middle of the above-chance range (middle performance), or higher within it (higher performance). In every scenario the probability of a correct response followed a chance-corrected logit with a .50 floor, a positive age effect, a group difference, and no age-by-group product term on the chance-corrected-logit scale. A subject random intercept corresponded to a latent-scale intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of .30. Each dataset contained `r sim_k` trial-level Bernoulli responses for each of $N = `r sim_N`$ participants, with age and group constant across a participant's trials.

Each simulated dataset was analyzed with four mixed models sharing the same subject random intercept: a Gaussian identity LMM applied to the binary trial outcome, standard binomial-logit and binomial-probit GLMMs, and the matched chance-corrected binomial-logit GLMM. The matched model was fitted with `lme4::glmer` and `psyphy::mafc.logit(2)` using 10 adaptive quadrature points (`nAGQ = 10`), because with the default Laplace approximation (`nAGQ = 1`) nearly half of its fits had numerical problems (Supplement A). Each model received one fit attempt. The primary rates are computed among fits that passed basic convergence checks. Rates among fits flagged for numerical problems are reported separately as apparent rejection rates, because their Wald tests can be unreliable (criteria in Supplement A).

![Simulation 1: forced-choice accuracy with a chance floor and a subject random intercept. The product term is zero on the conditional chance-corrected-logit scale. Panel A shows fixed-effect curves at random intercept 0 across three performance levels; the grey region lies below the .50 chance floor. Panel B shows the primary product-term rejection rates among fits passing the minimal fit-quality checks. The dashed line marks $\alpha = .05$.](../figs/forced-choice-simulation.pdf){#fig-forced-choice-simulation fig-pos="htbp"}

The matched chance-corrected model rejected the product term in `r fc_pct_range(fc_cc$"Primary rejection rate")` of acceptable fits. The alternative links produced pseudo-interactions, most often near the chance floor. In the lower-performance scenario the standard logit detected an interaction in `r fc_rate("Lower performance", "Standard binomial logit")`% of replications, the standard probit in `r fc_rate("Lower performance", "Standard binomial probit")`%, and the Gaussian identity in `r fc_rate("Lower performance", "Gaussian identity")`%. In the higher-performance scenario these rates fell to `r fc_rate("Higher performance", "Standard binomial logit")`%, `r fc_rate("Higher performance", "Standard binomial probit")`%, and `r fc_rate("Higher performance", "Gaussian identity")`%.

In contrast, the Gaussian identity model remained at about the nominal level in the middle- and higher-performance scenarios (`r fc_rate("Middle performance", "Gaussian identity")`% and `r fc_rate("Higher performance", "Gaussian identity")`%). Between .50 and 1, the generating curve is S-shaped and almost linear around .75. When the cells fall on both sides of .75, its flattening near the floor and near the ceiling roughly cancel, so effects also add up on the probability scale.

The matched model was the hardest to fit. Even with `nAGQ = 10`, from `r fc_pct_range(fc_cc$"Fit-problem rate")` of its fits were flagged, against at most `r round(100 * max(fc_alt$"Fit-problem rate"))`% for the alternatives. Flagged fits are not a minor nuisance here, because they rejected the product term in `r fc_pct_range(fc_cc$"Apparent rejection rate, flagged fits")` of cases. An analyst who ignored the warnings would therefore obtain a pseudo-interaction rate of `r fc_pct_range(fc_cc_pooled)` from the model that is correct by construction, comparable to some of the wrong links. The chance-corrected link is the ideal solution in principle, but in a GLMM it requires attention to fitting options and convergence warnings.

## Within-Family Link Choice

In the forced-choice case the standard link was wrong for the task by construction, because it placed the lower asymptote at 0 when the design fixed it at chance. The link-function problem can also arise in less obvious cases. Logit and probit are both standard for binary data, respect the same 0-to-1 bounds, and usually produce very similar fitted probabilities. They differ mainly in interpretation, since logit coefficients are log-odds, whereas probit coefficients are expressed on a standard-normal latent scale, which makes probit the usual choice when modeling psychological quantities such as ability, signal strength, and response tendency [@dunn2018]. The choice between them is therefore often guided by convention, interpretation, or software, with little expected impact on substantive conclusions [@yuhuang2019; @agresti2002]. Yet even two nearly interchangeable links define slightly different scales of additivity. Equal differences under one link are not exactly equal under the other, especially toward the tails, and this alone can alter the estimated product term.

### Simulation 2: Design and Results

```{r}
#| label: within-family-inline
#| include: false

# Design constants for Simulation 2 (see scripts/03b-simulation-within-family-links.R).
wf_N <- 700
wf_k <- 15
n_rep_wf <- max(within_family_sim$`Successful fits`)

wf_lookup <- function(gen, fit, col) {
  require_single(
    within_family_sim[
      within_family_sim$`Generating link` == gen & within_family_sim$`Fitted link` == fit,
      col, drop = TRUE
    ],
    paste0("within_family_sim[", gen, " / ", fit, " / ", col, "]")
  )
}
wf_rejection_rate <- function(gen, fit) round(100 * wf_lookup(gen, fit, "Rejection rate"))
wf_induced_product <- function(gen, fit) fmt_num(wf_lookup(gen, fit, "Induced product term"), 3)
```

Simulation 2 asks whether swapping two links that share the binomial family and the 0-to-1 bounds produces pseudo-interactions. The two scenarios differ in the generating link, logit or probit. In both, repeated binary responses were generated in a two-group, two-condition design with no condition-by-group product term on the generating link scale and a subject random intercept (latent ICC = .30). The two scenarios were constructed to give almost the same four cell probabilities. Each dataset contained $N = `r wf_N`$ participants with `r wf_k` trials per participant-condition cell. This sample is larger than in a typical psychological study and was chosen so that the small systematic discrepancy between the two links would be detectable. Each dataset was fitted with a random-intercept GLMM under both links, so that every generating link was crossed with every fitted link. @fig-within-family-links shows the results, and Supplement A tabulates the full crossed-link rates.

![Simulation 2: logit versus probit in repeated-trial random-intercept GLMMs. Data are generated with no condition-by-group product term on the generating link scale. Panel A shows the cell probabilities under each generating link. Both links give almost the same probabilities, and the grey lines mark equal steps on each link scale. Panel B shows product-term rejection rates for each generating–fitted link combination. Error bars are Wilson 95% confidence intervals; the dashed line marks $\alpha = .05$.](../figs/within-family-links.pdf){#fig-within-family-links fig-pos="htbp"}

When the fitted link matches the generating link, the nominal rejection rate stays near .05, at `r wf_rejection_rate("logit", "logit")`% for logit fitted to logit-generated data and `r wf_rejection_rate("probit", "probit")`% for probit fitted to probit-generated data. Crossing the links raises the pseudo-interaction detection rate to `r wf_rejection_rate("probit", "logit")`% when a logit model is fitted to probit-generated data and `r wf_rejection_rate("logit", "probit")`% when a probit model is fitted to logit-generated data. 

These rates reflect a fixed quantity. Under the wrong link, the same cell probabilities imply a small but nonzero product term on the fitted scale, against exactly zero when the links match (Supplement A, Section S5). How often this term is detected depends on where the four cell probabilities lie between 0 and 1, and Supplement B shows that the same link mismatch is nearly undetectable at some probability levels and much easier to detect at others.

## Sum Scores

Many psychological outcomes are computed as total sum scores across questionnaire items, task items, symptoms, errors, or ratings. In the two cases above the outcome was a directly observed response, and only the link was in question. A sum score is different, because the score itself is already the result of an analytic choice. What is observed are the individual item responses, which are binary or ordinal; the total is a summary of them, produced by a scoring rule that gives every item the same weight and every point of the scale the same width. In psychological research the construct of interest is often the underlying, generally continuous dimension, so the total can be seen as a remapped version of that continuum. The link question then arrives together with a prior question about which metric the claim is about.

The bounds matter because the construct may have no floor or ceiling, whereas the total score has both. The relation between the two can be described by how much change on the latent dimension is needed to raise the total by one point, and this amount is not constant. In the middle of the score range a small latent change moves the total by a point, because many items are close to changing category. Near either bound a much larger latent change is needed, because most items are already at their lowest or highest category. A constant latent effect therefore translates into fewer raw-score points as the total approaches the floor or the ceiling, and the same holds wherever the instrument is less informative along the latent dimension, so the effect is not limited to the endpoints. A Gaussian identity model fitted to the total assumes the opposite, namely that a predictor shifts the score by the same number of points at every level of the other predictor. When one group lies closer to a bound, a predictor with the same latent effect in both groups moves that group's score by fewer points, and the model reports the difference as an interaction.

The problem we raise sits next to a recent, wider debate about whether sum scores should be replaced by factor scores or latent-variable models. Some argue that sum scores are transparent, reliable enough for many purposes, comparable across studies, and tied to how instruments are scored in applied settings [@widaman2023]; the counterargument is that a total encodes strong and usually untested assumptions about how items represent the construct [@mcneish2020; @mcneish2023]. Without entering that debate, we add a narrower point that it leaves aside. A model of the manifest total defines the absence of an interaction in raw-score points, so an interaction found there is an interaction on the score, and it becomes a claim about the construct only under the additional assumption that the two are linearly related.

When item-level data are available, the measurement model itself can instead be modeled explicitly [@burknervuorre2019]. Often, however, researchers deliberately work with the total score for the practical reasons listed above. One option is then a family that respects the bounds and the discreteness of the total, for example a beta-binomial likelihood for a bounded count [@wilcox1981]. Here we use a deliberately unusual alternative that changes only the link, keeping the observed total under a Gaussian likelihood, rescaling it to the proportion of the maximum score, and applying a probit link, as in Simulation 3 below. This *ad hoc* device is outside standard practice. It shows whether the interaction conclusion changes when additivity is placed on a scale that compresses expected values toward the score bounds. It remains a model of the total and will not recover the construct, and its Gaussian likelihood still ignores that the variance of a bounded score depends on its mean. It is a precaution for researchers who analyze totals anyway and accept that the interaction still needs a scale on which additivity is plausible.

### Simulation 3: Design and Results

```{r}
#| label: sum-score-inline
#| include: false

# Design constants for Simulation 3 (see scripts/03c-simulation-sum-scores.R).
ss_N   <- 600
ss_J   <- 9
ss_cat <- 3                 # each item scored 0 to 3
ss_max <- ss_J * ss_cat     # 0-27 total
n_rep_ss <- max(sum_score_sim$`Successful fits`)

ss_lookup <- function(scn, mdl, col) {
  require_single(
    sum_score_sim[
      sum_score_sim$Scenario == scn & sum_score_sim$Model == mdl,
      col, drop = TRUE
    ],
    paste0("sum_score_sim[", scn, " / ", mdl, " / ", col, "]")
  )
}
ss_rejection_rate <- function(scn, mdl) round(100 * ss_lookup(scn, mdl, "Rejection rate"))

# Ranges quoted in the text are the observed min/max across scenarios, so they
# stay ordered if a re-run changes which scenario is the extreme one.
ss_rate_range <- function(mdl) {
  rates <- sum_score_sim$`Rejection rate`[sum_score_sim$Model == mdl]
  if (length(rates) == 0) stop("No rejection rates found for model ", mdl, ".")
  round(100 * range(rates))
}
ss_rate_min <- function(mdl) ss_rate_range(mdl)[1]
ss_rate_max <- function(mdl) ss_rate_range(mdl)[2]
```

Simulation 3 asks whether a sum score shows an interaction that is absent on the latent scale it summarizes. Three scenarios shifted the item thresholds so that expected totals fell in the lower, middle, or upper part of the score range. In every scenario a continuous latent variable depended on a continuous predictor $x$ and a group effect, with no x-by-group product term. The latent values generated `r ss_J` ordinal items scored 0 to `r ss_cat`, which were summed to a total ranging from 0 to `r ss_max`. Each dataset contained $N = `r ss_N`$ participants.

We analyzed each total in three ways: a Gaussian identity model of the observed sum score, a Gaussian-probit bounded-score model, and the true latent generating scale. The bounded-score model applies a probit link to a continuity-corrected score proportion and rescales predictions to the original sum-score metric. We used probit because its standard-normal linear predictor provides a simple correspondence with the latent scale. Results are shown in @fig-sum-score-simulation, with per-scenario rates in Supplement A, Section S4.

![Simulation 3: sum scores as bounded and discrete outcomes. Data are generated with no x-by-group product term on the latent scale. Panel A shows how the same additive latent structure maps onto sum scores in the lower, middle, and upper parts of the score range. Panel B shows product-term rejection rates for the latent benchmark, which is available only in simulation, and two observed-score models. The dashed line marks $\alpha = .05$.](../figs/sum-score-simulation.pdf){#fig-sum-score-simulation fig-pos="htbp"}

The latent benchmark remained close to the nominal .05 rejection rate in every scenario, from `r ss_rate_min("Latent generating scale")`% to `r ss_rate_max("Latent generating scale")`%. The identity model rejected in `r ss_rejection_rate("Lower range", "Observed sum-score identity")`% of replications in the lower range, `r ss_rejection_rate("Middle range", "Observed sum-score identity")`% in the middle range, and `r ss_rejection_rate("Upper range", "Observed sum-score identity")`% in the upper range, so it came closest to the nominal rate in the middle, where the sum score is approximately linear in the latent variable, and its rate rose as expected totals approached a bound. The bounded-score probit model rejected in `r ss_rejection_rate("Lower range", "Gaussian-probit bounded score")`%, `r ss_rejection_rate("Middle range", "Gaussian-probit bounded score")`%, and `r ss_rejection_rate("Upper range", "Gaussian-probit bounded score")`% of replications in the same three ranges.

Across the broader scenarios in Supplement B, the position of expected scores within the range affected identity-model rejection much more than sample size, item count, or latent dispersion. Raw-score additivity can thus approximate latent-scale additivity when scores remain away from the bounds, and the bounded-score probit model can serve as a sensitivity analysis when they do not. For claims about interactions between latent constructs, an explicit measurement model provides a more direct approach, for example SEM, item-level ordinal models, or IRT-inspired models. These approaches still depend on assumptions about thresholds, links, loadings, and latent-response scales, but they make those assumptions explicit.

# Can Standard Diagnostics Flag a Wrong Link?

The simulations above assume that the analyst accepts the fitted model. In practice, a researcher who finds an interaction may check the model before reporting it. We examined three checks based on different strategies. A Pregibon-style link test probes the assumed link, residual diagnostics screen for misfit of any kind, and AIC compares candidate models.

The Pregibon test refits the model adding the squared fitted linear predictor, $\hat{\eta}^2$, as a predictor [@pregibon1980]. If the link is adequate, this term adds no information. A significant coefficient indicates curvature that the link does not explain. For residual diagnostics, we used the simulated quantile residuals of DHARMa [@hartig2024; see also @dunnsmyth1996]. Under an adequate model they are uniform between 0 and 1, whatever the family. Misfit appears as non-uniformity, over- or underdispersion, or patterns over fitted values and predictors. AIC compares only the models it is given. In our simulation the candidate models differ only in the link, so they have the same number of parameters and AIC ranks them by log-likelihood alone.

None of the above checks is specific to the link. A significant Pregibon term targets the link, but it also flags any omitted nonlinearity or interaction. Moreover, the product term absorbs part of the curvature produced by a wrong link. With a continuous predictor, some curvature remains within groups and can in principle be detected. In a saturated $2 \times 2$ design no curvature remains in the fixed effects, because any link can reproduce the four cell means.

The monotonic linear model of @dunnanderson2026 tests scale dependence more directly, asking whether additivity can be recovered under any monotonic transformation. All pseudo-interactions simulated here are removable in this sense. We did not include the test, because it requires cell-level data from a factorial design, whereas most of our scenarios include continuous predictors, trial-level random effects, or both.

## Diagnostic Simulation

This simulation asks whether standard post-fit checks distinguish a wrong-link model from the correct one. Its five scenarios are based on examples introduced earlier, with sample sizes and coefficients reported in Supplement A. Each keeps the outcome family and the interaction formula fixed, so the fitted model is wrong about the scale on which effects add and about nothing else. *Count errors* follows the Poisson-log example of @fig-simple-count-example and fits it with an identity link. *Chance-floor accuracy* takes the lower-performance scenario of Simulation 1, with trial-level responses and a subject random intercept, and compares standard-logit and chance-corrected-logit GLMMs with the same random effects. *Binary repeated trials* follows the probit-generated, logit-fitted case of Simulation 2 with `r dg_N_binary` participants instead of `r wf_N`. *Binary continuous predictor* repeats that case with a continuous predictor instead of the two-level condition, so that residual patterns can be examined along a predictor. *Gamma mean response time* generates response times from a Gamma model with a log link and fits the inverse link.

In each of 3,000 replications per scenario we fitted two models to the same data, one with the wrong link and one with the correct (generating) link. The wrong-link model is the one an analyst would inspect after finding a significant interaction. We applied the Pregibon test and the residual checks, run with the DHARMa defaults (version 0.5.0), to both models, because a check is informative about the link only if it flags the wrong-link model more often than the correct one. AIC compared the two models directly. @tbl-diagnostic-scenarios reports the rates for both models side by side. Each rate is computed over the replications in which the check could be computed, for example excluding fits that failed, and Supplement A reports these denominators. The scenarios illustrate how the checks behave in the cases studied above, and Supplement B extends them across sample sizes and effect sizes.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diagnostic-scenarios
#| tbl-colwidths: [20, 21, 11, 21, 15, 12]
#| tbl-cap: "Diagnostic simulation across five link-misspecification scenarios."
#| apa-note: "In each replication the same data were fitted with the correct (generating) link and with a wrong link; family and formula were the same. Pseudo-interaction rate: proportion of replications in which the wrong-link model detected an interaction absent on the correct link scale. Correct / wrong link: flagging rate for the correct-link model / for the wrong-link model; a check is informative only if the second rate clearly exceeds the first. DHARMa: range across the four residual checks, run with package defaults. Pregibon: added-term link check; N.I. = not identifiable in the saturated $2 \\times 2$ design, where the squared linear predictor is collinear with the fixed effects. AIC prefers correct link: proportion of replications in which the correct-link model had the lower AIC; the two models have the same number of parameters, so indistinguishable links would give about .50. Denominators and confidence intervals are reported in Supplement A."
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  diagnostic_scenario_display_table(diagnostic_scenarios),
  align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

Only in the count scenario did the checks reliably detect the wrong link. There, the Pregibon test flagged it in `r dg_pct("Count errors", "Pregibon check")`% of replications and the residual checks in up to `r dg_pct("Count errors", "DHARMa max")`%, with the quantile check over the focal predictor as the most sensitive (@fig-diagnostic-flagging). In the other four scenarios the residual checks flagged the wrong link in at most `r dg_max_other("DHARMa max")`% of replications. The same quantile check was again the most sensitive in the Gamma scenario, whereas in the three binomial scenarios no residual check separated the wrong link from the correct one. The Pregibon test flagged the wrong link in `r dg_pct("Gamma mean response time", "Pregibon check")`% of Gamma replications and `r dg_pct("Chance-floor accuracy", "Pregibon check")`% of chance-floor replications, and in the binary scenario with a continuous predictor it flagged it about as often as the correct link (`r dg_pct("Binary continuous predictor", "Pregibon check")`%). AIC preferred the correct link in `r dg_range("AIC favors target")` of replications. It gave the most consistent signal of the three checks, but only because the correct link was among the candidates.

![Share of replications in which each DHARMa residual check flagged the model at $\alpha = .05$, by check (rows of panels) and scenario (colors and shapes). Open symbols show the correct-link model and filled symbols the wrong-link model fitted to the same data. A check is informative about the link only when the filled symbol lies clearly to the right of the open one. The x-axis uses a square-root scale to spread the low rates, and the dashed line marks .05.](../figs/diagnostic-flagging.pdf){#fig-diagnostic-flagging fig-pos="htbp"}

The chance-floor scenario is the most instructive. The wrong-link model produced pseudo-interactions in `r dg_pct("Chance-floor accuracy", "Pseudo-interaction detection")`% of replications, yet the residual checks flagged it in at most `r dg_pct("Chance-floor accuracy", "DHARMa max")`%. Applied to the correct chance-corrected model, they flagged it in up to `r cal_cf_dharma_max`%, and the Pregibon test in `r cal_cf_pregibon`%, slightly more often than the wrong-link model. Here the checks thus pointed, if anything, toward the wrong model, whereas in all other scenarios no check flagged more than `r cal_other_max`% of correct-link models. In the two logit-probit scenarios the stakes were lower, because pseudo-interactions occurred in only `r dg_pct("Binary repeated trials", "Pseudo-interaction detection")`% and `r dg_pct("Binary continuous predictor", "Pseudo-interaction detection")`% of replications.

The larger grid of Supplement B confirms this pattern. In the count and Gamma scenarios, the Pregibon test flagged the wrong link more often as pseudo-interactions became more frequent, while flagging the correct link at about the nominal rate. In the three binomial scenarios, no residual check flagged the wrong link more than one percentage point more often than the correct one, and larger samples made the checks flag both links more often. The Pregibon test separated the two chance-floor models only with 500 or more participants or at the highest intercept.

# From Link Choice to Sensitivity Analysis

In practice, an interaction analysis should state the three choices it depends on: the outcome family, the link that defines additivity, and the metric the claim refers to. It should also test whether its conclusion holds under plausible alternatives (@tbl-link-aware-workflow). Sometimes the observed metric is the relevant target. For example, a two-point difference on a clinical or educational score may be what matters in practice, and additivity in raw-score units may then be reasonable. The point is that this is a substantive choice, which should be made deliberately and reported. When possible, the link should be justified by theory, task structure, or measurement.

When the link can affect the interaction conclusion, we suggest a sensitivity analysis across plausible links as the main robustness check. The removability test of @dunnanderson2026 addresses the same problem across all monotonic transformations of the outcome, but it does not decide which transformations are admissible. The family, the bounds, the chance level, and the meaning of the outcome strongly restrict the plausible mappings. We suggest testing the interaction under each defensible link, reporting the corresponding response-scale contrast, and stating whether the conclusion is stable or depends on the link. If it depends on the link, this should be disclosed [@mccabe2022; @mize2019; @rohrer2026; @mustillo2018].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-link-aware-workflow
#| tbl-cap: "Practical starting points for link-aware interaction testing across common psychological outcomes."
#| tbl-colwidths: [20, 42, 38]
#| echo: false

workflow <- data.frame(
  `Outcome type` = c(
    "Forced-choice accuracy",
    "Binary / proportion outcome",
    "Likert / ordinal item",
    "Sum score / composite",
    "Counts / error counts",
    "Response time / skewed positive outcome"
  ),
  `Plausible starting point` = c(
    "Binomial logit/probit; chance-corrected link when the task floor is part of the estimand.",
    "Binomial logit/probit; consider cloglog for asymmetric processes.",
    "Ordinal logit/probit; metric model only with a clear observed-scale target.",
    "Gaussian identity when many levels stay far from bounds; otherwise consider item-level, ordinal, bounded-count, or bounded-score models.",
    "Poisson or negative binomial, usually with log link; identity only with an observed-count target.",
    "Lognormal, Gamma log/inverse, Inverse Gaussian, or transformed Gaussian, matched to absolute, proportional, reciprocal, or transformed change."
  ),
  `Minimal sensitivity check` = c(
    "Compare standard logit/probit and chance-corrected links; report convergence and response-scale contrasts.",
    "Compare logit/probit; inspect calibration and contrasts near bounds or rare-event regions.",
    "Compare ordinal and metric summaries; report category probabilities or response-scale contrasts.",
    "Inspect bounds, skew, and score concentration; compare with item-level or bounded-score sensitivity models when feasible.",
    "Check overdispersion and zero inflation; compare count contrasts across plausible count models.",
    "Compare raw-, log-, and response-scale summaries; inspect tail fit and predicted values."
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(workflow, align = c("l", "l", "l"))
```

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

# Discussion and conclusions

The same data can support different interaction conclusions under different plausible specifications, which is the familiar scale dependence of interactions [@cox1984; @dunnanderson2026; @loftus1978; @wagenmakers2012]. In a GLM that dependence is carried by two choices, the outcome family and the link function. Our review found interaction tests to be common in all five journals sampled, the link function usually left implicit, and identity-link analyses applied to many outcomes for which observed-scale additivity is not self-evident.

The simulations showed how link misspecification affects interaction tests. With two main effects present, a link that misplaces additivity turned a purely additive generating process into a significant product term even when the outcome family was correct. In forced-choice accuracy the binomial family is correct and, in the simulated process, the error lies entirely in a canonical link that places the lower asymptote at 0 when it should be at the chance level. The matched chance-corrected model, however, was the hardest to fit, and its flagged fits produced spurious interactions in most cases, so even fitting the correct model may require caution. The logit-probit comparison showed that the problem survives when the response bounds are correct as well, between two links that look alike over most of the range. In the sum-score case the choice extends beyond the link to the outcome itself. A total is a scoring rule applied to item responses, so an interaction estimated on it refers to raw-score points, and adopting a family that respects the bounds and the discreteness of the total still leaves open whether additivity in points stands for additivity in the construct.

Work on interaction testing has emphasized the large samples needed for adequate power [@baranger2023] and stable effect estimates [@castillo2026]. Larger samples reduce sampling variability, but they do not resolve scale dependence, a limitation that @castillo2026 also explicitly acknowledge. In our simulations, the wrong link induces a nonzero product term even though the generating process is additive. A larger sample estimates that term more precisely and detects it more often. Thus, a stable and well-powered interaction estimate can still refer to a different scale from the one intended by the substantive claim.

The diagnostic simulation asked whether ordinary post-fit checks flag link misspecification. Outside the count scenario, residual checks rarely detected the wrong link, and the Pregibon test did so in at most a third of replications. In the chance-floor case the checks even flagged the correct model slightly more often than the wrong one, so a clean diagnostic report did not mean that the scale was right. These checks assess fit, and AIC can only rank the links it is given. Whether an interaction claim holds on the scale the researcher means is a separate question [@dunnsmyth1996; @hartig2024; @pregibon1980].

The present study has three main limitations. First, the review is descriptive and it covers five prominent journals across major areas of psychology in a single recent year, so its estimates describe reporting practice in such outlets rather than the field as a whole. A broader review across journals, years, and subfields would be needed to support reporting guidance. Second, the review coded observable reporting features and did not assess whether each interaction was removable. Finally, the simulations demonstrate a mechanism. They target a single regime, in which two established main effects push expected values into the region where link curvature is strongest, and they cannot establish how often that situation arises or capture the further complications of real data.

Interaction claims therefore require an explicit scale. Before testing an interaction, researchers should decide which family suits the response, which link defines additivity, and which metric the claim concerns. After testing it, they should check whether the conclusion survives other defensible links. A conclusion that changes across these links can still be reported, as long as it is presented as conditional on the scale on which it was estimated.
